title: Trump Demands Permanent Iran Deal, Warns Next Move Could Be Delayed Until 2027【Live Updates】
body:
President Donald Trump told an Israeli media outlet on Friday that his administration is still weighing a “permanent” diplomatic arrangement with Tehran, but he added that any decisive step in the ongoing Iran‑U.S. confrontation could be delayed until as late as 2027. The remarks came as Israel’s nascent government, still in the throes of coalition talks, grappled with internal divisions over how to respond to the heightened regional tension.

Trump’s comments were made during an interview with the Israeli newspaper *Israel Hayom*, where he reiterated his belief that a long‑term settlement with Iran is possible if Washington can secure a “real, binding, permanent deal.” However, he cautioned that the United States might not be ready to act on a new strategy for several years, citing the need for “more time to evaluate the options and the consequences.” The statement has sparked a fresh round of debate among policymakers in Washington and Jerusalem, who are already wrestling with the implications of a protracted diplomatic deadlock.

The timing of the president’s remarks is significant. In the past month, the United States has intensified its pressure campaign against Iran, imposing additional sanctions on the country’s nuclear and ballistic‑missile programs while conducting a series of naval patrols in the Persian Gulf. Tehran, for its part, has continued to advance its uranium enrichment capacity and has threatened retaliation if the United States proceeds with what it calls “unlawful aggression.” The prospect of a delayed U.S. response could embolden Iran to further expand its regional influence, potentially destabilizing fragile ceasefires in Syria, Yemen and Lebanon.

In Jerusalem, the political landscape is equally volatile. Gadi Eisenkot, the veteran former chief of staff who has been tasked with assembling a new coalition after the recent elections, warned that his broad‑based bloc must avoid protracted negotiations that could stall governance. Eisenkot’s coalition includes parties ranging from right‑wing nationalists to centrist moderates, each with divergent views on Iran. While some factions advocate a hardline stance, calling for immediate military readiness and a robust deterrence posture, others push for renewed diplomatic overtures and a return to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) framework. The internal friction underscores the difficulty Israel faces in forming a coherent policy toward Tehran, especially as it seeks to balance security concerns with the desire to avoid another costly war.

Analysts note that Trump’s suggestion of a 2027 timeline may be a strategic move to buy political capital domestically. By framing the issue as a long‑term challenge, the administration can deflect immediate criticism over its handling of the Iran situation while positioning itself for future negotiations that could be leveraged in upcoming electoral cycles. Moreover, the extended horizon provides Washington with a window to coordinate with regional allies—particularly Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates—on a multilateral approach that could incorporate economic incentives alongside security guarantees.

Nevertheless, the notion of postponing a decisive U.S. move carries risks. Prolonged uncertainty could erode confidence among U.S. allies, especially Israel, which relies heavily on American military support. It may also allow Iran to consolidate its nuclear advancements and deepen ties with proxy groups across the Middle East, complicating any future diplomatic overtures. The longer the United States waits, the more intricate the diplomatic puzzle becomes, potentially limiting the leverage Washington can exert in any eventual settlement.

Looking ahead, the coming months will be critical for both Washington and Jerusalem. As Israel’s coalition talks inch toward a final agreement, the new government’s stance on Iran will likely shape the regional security calculus. Simultaneously, the United States must decide whether to maintain its current pressure campaign, pursue renewed negotiations, or adopt a hybrid strategy that blends sanctions with diplomatic outreach. The trajectory of these decisions will determine whether the “permanent” deal Trump envisions remains a distant aspiration or becomes an actionable policy within the next few years.
